lessons.title: Greetings and introductions
lessons.objective: Greet people, introduce yourself and exchange simple personal information in English.

content.heading: Greetings
content.text: In English, « Hello » and « Hi » are used to greet. « Good morning » is said in the morning, « Good afternoon » in the afternoon and « Good evening » in the evening. To take leave: « Goodbye » or « Bye » (informal).

content.heading: Introducing yourself
content.text: To give your name: « My name is … » or « I'm … ». To ask: « What is your name? ». Ask how someone is with « How are you? », reply: « I'm fine, thank you ».

content.heading: Pronouns and the verb be
content.text: The verb « to be » is essential: I am (I'm), you are (you're), he/she/it is, we are, they are. Examples: « I am a student », « She is a teacher », « We are friends ».

exercises.question: How do you greet someone in English?
How do you say "my name is Anna"?
What does "I am a student" mean?

lessons.audioScript:
Anna: Hello! My name is Anna. What is your name?
Ben: Hi Anna! I'm Ben. Nice to meet you.
Anna: Nice to meet you too. How are you?
Ben: I'm fine, thank you. And you?

lessons.title: The alphabet and sounds
lessons.objective: Spell your name and recognise the basic sounds of English.

content.heading: The alphabet
content.text: The English alphabet has 26 letters. To spell, you say each letter: « A », « B », « C ». The most difficult sounds for learners are often « H », pronounced « aitch », and « R », pronounced « ar ».

content.heading: The vowels
content.text: The five vowels A, E, I, O, U have several pronunciations. « A » can be said as in « cat », « name » or « father ». Each word must be learned with its pronunciation.

content.heading: Spelling a name
content.text: To spell on the phone, one often specifies: « B for Bravo », « M for Mike ». This is the radio alphabet convention, useful to avoid confusion.

exercises.question: How many letters does the English alphabet have?
How is the letter « R » pronounced in English?
What does "to spell" mean?

lessons.audioScript:
Receptionist: Can you spell your last name, please?
Anna: Yes, it's M-U-L-L-E-R.
Receptionist: Thank you. M-U-L-L-E-R.
Anna: That's right!

lessons.title: Numbers
lessons.objective: Count, give your age and your phone number in English.

content.heading: Numbers from 0 to 20
content.text: The basic numbers: zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Then eleven (11), twelve (12), thirteen (13) up to twenty (20).

content.heading: The tens
content.text: The tens end in « -ty »: twenty (20), thirty (30), forty (40), fifty (50), sixty (60), seventy (70), eighty (80), ninety (90). Note that « fourty » is spelled « forty ».

content.heading: Compound numbers and age
content.text: For 21, say « twenty-one ». To give your age, English uses « to be » and not « to have »: « I am twenty years old ». A phone number is read digit by digit.

exercises.question: How do you say 20 in English?
How do you say "I am twenty years old"?
How do you say 30?

lessons.audioScript:
Ben: How old are you?
Anna: I am twenty-five years old. And you?
Ben: I am twenty-seven. What's your phone number?
Anna: It's 0-8-1-2-3-4-5-6.

lessons.title: The family
lessons.objective: Introduce your family and use the possessives my, your, his, her.

content.heading: Family members
content.text: Close relatives: father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter. The generic term « parents » refers to both parents.

content.heading: The extended family
content.text: Further: grandfather, grandmother, uncle, aunt, cousin. Say « grandparents » for the grandparents.

content.heading: Possessives
content.text: The possessive adjectives never change: my, your, his (masculine), her (feminine), our, their. Example: « my mother », « his brother », « their house ».

vocabulary.translation: the child of an uncle or aunt

exercises.question: How do you say "the mother" in English?
How do you say "my father"?
What does "his brother" mean?

lessons.audioScript:
Anna: Do you have brothers or sisters?
Ben: Yes, I have one brother and one sister. What about you?
Anna: I have two sisters. My mother is a teacher and my father is a doctor.

lessons.title: Daily routine
lessons.objective: Describe your daily activities and use the present simple.

content.heading: The morning
content.text: The day begins with « to wake up », « to get up » and « to have breakfast ». Say: « I wake up at six o'clock ».

content.heading: During the day
content.text: During the day: « to work », « to study », « to have lunch ». The time is given with « at »: « at eight o'clock », « at noon ».

content.heading: The present simple
content.text: The present simple describes habits: « I go to work », « He goes to school ». In the third person, the verb takes an « s »: work → works, go → goes. The negative: « I don't work on Sunday ».

vocabulary.translation: the early part of the day
the late part of the day

exercises.question: How do you say "to get up" in English?
How do you say "I work at eight o'clock"?
How is "to go" conjugated in the third person?

lessons.audioScript:
Ben: What time do you get up?
Anna: I wake up at six and I get up at six fifteen.
Ben: Do you have breakfast at home?
Anna: Yes, I have breakfast at seven, then I go to work at eight.

lessons.title: Food and drink
lessons.objective: Order food, express your tastes and use « would like ».

content.heading: Basic foods
content.text: Common foods: bread, rice, meat, chicken, fish, vegetables, fruit. Drinks: water, tea, coffee, milk, juice.

content.heading: At the restaurant
content.text: To order politely: « I would like … ». Example: « I would like a coffee, please ». Ask for the bill with « The bill, please ».

content.heading: Expressing your tastes
content.text: « To like » means to enjoy: « I like tea », negative « I don't like coffee ». « It's delicious ». « Would you like …? » offers something.

exercises.question: How do you say "bread" in English?
How do you order "a coffee, please"?
options: I would like a coffee, please
exercises.answer: I would like a coffee, please

exercises.question: How do you ask for the bill?

lessons.audioScript:
Waiter: What would you like?
Anna: I would like some rice and chicken, please.
Waiter: And to drink?
Anna: A glass of water, please. Thank you.

lessons.title: Housing
lessons.objective: Describe your home and use « there is / there are ».

content.heading: Types of housing
content.text: You live in « a house » or « an apartment/flat ». The rooms: the kitchen, the bedroom, the bathroom, the living room.

content.heading: Furniture
content.text: Essential furniture: the table, the chair, the bed, the wardrobe, the sofa. Describe with « there is » (singular) and « there are » (plural).

content.heading: Describing your home
content.text: Example: « There is a kitchen and there are two bedrooms in my apartment ». To ask: « How many rooms does your house have? ».

exercises.question: How do you say "an apartment" in English?
How do you say "there are two bedrooms"?
What does "the bathroom" mean?

lessons.audioScript:
Anna: Tell me about your apartment.
Ben: It's small but nice. There is one bedroom, a kitchen and a bathroom.
Anna: Is there a living room?
Ben: Yes, there is a small living room too.

lessons.title: Time and appointments
lessons.objective: Tell the time, the days of the week and make an appointment.

content.heading: The time
content.text: Ask the time with « What time is it? ». The reply: « It's three o'clock », « It's half past three », « It's quarter to four ».

content.heading: The days of the week
content.text: The days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. « Today », « tomorrow », « yesterday ».

content.heading: Making an appointment
content.text: For an appointment: « Let's meet at three o'clock ». The preposition « at » precedes the time, « on » the day: « on Monday at three ».

vocabulary.translation: the last day of the week

exercises.question: How do you ask the time?
What does "half past three" mean?
Which day is "Friday"?

lessons.audioScript:
Ben: What time is it?
Anna: It's half past two.
Ben: Let's meet on Friday at three.
Anna: OK, Friday at three. See you then!

lessons.title: Shopping
lessons.objective: Ask a price, buy and receive change in a shop.

content.heading: At the shop
content.text: The seller asks: « Can I help you? ». Reply: « I'm just looking, thank you » or « How much is this? ».

content.heading: Asking a price
content.text: « How much is it? » (singular) and « How much are they? » (plural). The price: « It's twenty pounds/dollars ». Clothes: a shirt, a dress, shoes.

content.heading: Paying
content.text: To pay: « Can I pay by card? » or « I'll pay in cash ». « Do you have a bigger size? » asks for a larger size.

exercises.question: How do you ask the price?
What does "cheap" mean?
How do you say "I'll take it"?

lessons.audioScript:
Anna: How much is this shirt?
Seller: It's twenty dollars.
Anna: OK, I'll take it. Can I pay by card?
Seller: Yes, of course. Here is your receipt.

lessons.title: Travel and transport
lessons.objective: Buy a ticket, use transport and ask for directions.

content.heading: Means of transport
content.text: Transport: the bus, the train, the plane, the taxi, the car. « To take the bus ». The station: the station, the airport: the airport.

content.heading: Buying a ticket
content.text: At the counter: « A ticket to London, please ». Specify « one-way » or « return ». « What time does the train leave? ».

content.heading: Asking for directions
content.text: To find your way: « Excuse me, where is the station? ». The directions: go straight, turn left, turn right.

exercises.question: How do you say "the train" in English?
How do you say "one-way"?
What does "turn left" mean?

lessons.audioScript:
Anna: Excuse me, where is the station?
Passer-by: Go straight, then turn left.
Anna: Go straight and turn left. Thank you!
Passer-by: You're welcome.
